script.title: The Con Man Who Sold the Eiffel Tower for Scrap
sentences: In 1925, a con man sold the Eiffel Tower for scrap.
Victor Lustig had read in a Paris newspaper that the tower was costly to maintain.
He had a forger make fake government stationery.
Posing as a government official, he met scrap metal dealers at an expensive hotel.
He said the government wished to sell the tower secretly, to avoid public outcry.
Dealer André Poisson paid a large bribe plus around 70,000 francs, and Lustig fled to Austria.
The twist: no newspaper reported the con, so Lustig returned and found a second buyer!
Would you have fallen for it?
script.description:
In 1925, Victor Lustig sold the Eiffel Tower for scrap.
Then he came back to sell it again.
claims_en: In 1925 Victor Lustig, a con artist, sold the Eiffel Tower to a scrap metal dealer in a scam.
In Paris he read a newspaper article about the problems of maintaining the Eiffel Tower; the city found it increasingly expensive to maintain and repaint.
He hired a forger to produce fake government stationery.
He invited scrap metal dealers to a confidential meeting at an expensive hotel, posing as a government official (Deputy Director-General of the Ministry of Posts and Telegraphs).
He told them the French government wished to sell the tower for scrap, and that nothing could be disclosed because the deal would likely spark public outcry.
André Poisson paid a large bribe and the funds for the sale, around 70,000 francs.
He could find no reference to the con in newspapers, so he returned to Paris to pull off the scheme again.
On the second attempt he found another mark willing to buy the Eiffel Tower.
